title: How Bluetooth pairs two devices and why it hops channels
description: Bluetooth devices swap secret keys when pairing, then hop across radio channels to dodge interference.

scenes.say: Two gadgets that have never met suddenly trust each other. How does Bluetooth pull that off?

steps: You confirm on screen or with a code
Keys are saved: this is bonding
scenes.say: That's pairing. The devices create shared secret keys, often with you confirming a number or passkey, which helps block a man in the middle. Saving those keys is called bonding, so they can trust each other next time.
Then they talk over the crowded two point four gigahertz band, which is unlicensed, so lots of gadgets use it. That makes interference a real problem.
To dodge interference, Bluetooth hops between channels. Classic uses seventy-nine. Low Energy uses forty, three for advertising, and thirty-seven for data.
It can even adapt, keeping a map of good and bad channels and avoiding the noisy ones. Two devices, one shared secret, and a constant dance across the radio band. Follow for more wireless explainers.
